definition: Rhapsodize means to engage in excessive enthusiasm.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rhapsodize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rhapsodize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Get Grandpa started on his old orchard and he will rhapsodize until the porch light comes on.
To mention a thing is to spend one sentence on it and move on — the far, quiet end of this scale; rhapsodizing lives at the other end entirely.
To enthuse is real, audible excitement, but rhapsodizing is stronger and longer than enthusing — praise settling in for the evening, with imagery.

To gush is to spill over-eager praise in one quick burst — a splash of superlatives, then done. To rhapsodize is longer-winded and more elaborate: the praise builds images and settles in. A gush is over in a breath; rhapsodizing wants the whole evening.

To rave is to praise at top volume — wild, emphatic, and brief enough that a critic can rave in a single sentence. To rhapsodize trades volume for altitude and length: image after image, praise that unspools. A rave is a shout; a rhapsody is a recital.

Rhapsodize means to engage in excessive enthusiasm.
Our sommelier began to rhapsodize about the '09 vintage — comparing it to a cello, then to October, then to a small cathedral — while the soup went quietly cold.
To rhapsodize is to praise at length and altitude — talk that has left the ground and doesn't want to land.
It is intransitive: you rhapsodize about or over something.
The gusher enjoys it more than the listener, which is the word's gentle joke.
Rhapsodize gently teases while it praises: it says the speaker's enthusiasm has become a performance.
Use it for the friend who cannot stop describing the ramen.
Gush is quicker and wetter; rave is louder; extol (in this unit's reference list) is the sober, formal cousin — you extol to persuade a committee, you rhapsodize because you can't help it.
